book: The Infinite Book of Big Secrets

stories.title: A 500-year-old note confirmed the Mona Lisa's identity
stories.summary: A margin note written in 1503 confirmed that Leonardo was working on a portrait of Lisa del Giocondo. Scholars published the discovery in 2005; Heidelberg announced its importance widely in 2008.
stories.full: For centuries, the identity of the Mona Lisa's sitter was debated, though the painter-biographer Giorgio Vasari had named Lisa del Giocondo in 1550. In an early printed edition of Cicero, a librarian at Heidelberg found a handwritten note by Florentine official Agostino Vespucci. The note, dated October 1503, refers to Leonardo painting Lisa del Giocondo. Heidelberg's library published the find in an exhibition catalogue in 2005 and publicized the confirmation in January 2008. That distinction matters: scholars did not first guess her identity in 2008; they obtained unusually strong contemporary evidence.
stories.sourceTitle: Heidelberg University Library

stories.title: The elephant Edison supposedly killed to prove a point
stories.summary: Topsy was electrocuted at Coney Island in 1903. Contrary to the popular story, historical evidence does not show Thomas Edison ordered the event or staged it to win the current wars.
stories.full: On January 4, 1903, the elephant Topsy was killed at Coney Island through a combination of electrocution and other methods. The disturbing event was filmed by an Edison-branded motion-picture company, and it is often retold as an AC-versus-DC stunt personally arranged by Thomas Edison. Rutgers historians find no contemporaneous evidence linking Edison personally to the decision, and the commercial war between alternating and direct current had largely ended by then. This is a story about a real event and how a compelling but misleading historical explanation spread afterward.
stories.sourceTitle: Thomas A. Edison Papers, Rutgers University

stories.title: A Toronto group invented a ghost named Philip
stories.summary: In the 1970s, researchers made up a fictional ghost's biography and reported mysterious raps during séances. The story is a documented experiment—not proof they created a real ghost.
stories.full: A Toronto parapsychology group headed by George and Iris Owen invented an imaginary historical character named Philip. Participants supplied him with a fictional past, gathered repeatedly and tried to communicate with him. They reported table movements and tapping responses during sessions. The group's own published accounts interpreted the reported events in paranormal terms, but those interpretations are not established scientific findings. What is historically verifiable is the experiment, its invented character and the researchers' recorded claims. The distinction between a curious experiment and proof of supernatural forces should remain visible on the card.
stories.sourceTitle: Survival Research Institute of Canada archive

stories.title: The reported ghosts of the White House
stories.summary: White House employees and visitors have told ghost stories for generations, especially about Abraham Lincoln. The historical reports are real; the apparitions are unverified.
stories.full: The White House Historical Association records a long tradition of supernatural stories from residents, employees and visitors. Jeremiah 'Jerry' Smith, a longtime White House worker, told reporters stories of seeing the spirit of Abraham Lincoln and others. Later tales attributed sightings to prominent visitors. These claims are significant as presidential folklore, especially because their sources and dates can be traced. They should not be presented as independent confirmation that ghosts exist.
stories.sourceTitle: White House Historical Association

stories.title: Steve Jobs introduced the iPhone as three products in one
stories.summary: Apple's January 9, 2007 launch framed iPhone as a phone, widescreen iPod and internet communicator. That original announcement also explains the emphasis on finger-driven multitouch.
stories.full: At Macworld in January 2007, Apple introduced the first iPhone with an unusual framing: a mobile phone, a widescreen iPod and an internet communications device merged into one. Apple's archived press release emphasized a multitouch interface that people could operate with their fingers rather than a stylus. The original positioning shows what Apple believed would be most surprising at the time, before the App Store and today's smartphone ecosystem reshaped expectations.
stories.sourceTitle: Apple Newsroom, January 9 2007

stories.title: On Venus, one rotation lasts longer than one year
stories.summary: Venus needs about 243 Earth days to rotate once but about 225 Earth days to orbit the Sun. Because it rotates backward, the Sun rises in the west.
stories.full: Venus rotates so slowly that a full spin takes approximately 243 Earth days. Its journey around the Sun takes about 225 Earth days, meaning one sidereal day is longer than its year. The planet also rotates in the opposite direction from most planets. One subtlety: sunrise-to-sunrise is not 243 days, because the planet is orbiting while it rotates; a solar day on Venus is about 117 Earth days. NASA's explanation makes this a perfect surprising fact with an important scientific distinction.
stories.sourceTitle: NASA Science: Venus facts

stories.title: A real moth appeared in a computer bug log
stories.summary: In 1947, Harvard Mark II engineers found a moth in a relay and taped it into the logbook. Engineers had already used the word 'bug' long before that.
stories.full: The famous 1947 Harvard Mark II logbook contains a moth discovered inside a computer component, labelled as an actual bug. The Smithsonian preserves the logbook. It's a wonderful origin story, but the word 'bug' for technical trouble predates the moth by many decades; Thomas Edison used the term during the nineteenth century. The historic surprise is that a team encountered a literal insect while diagnosing a machine and recorded it for posterity.
stories.sourceTitle: Smithsonian National Museum of American History

stories.title: A wave of molasses devastated Boston
stories.summary: A huge molasses tank burst in Boston in January 1919. The flood raced through the North End, killed 21 people and injured about 150.
stories.full: On January 15, 1919, a giant storage tank burst in Boston's North End, unleashing an immense surge of molasses. It struck buildings, vehicles and pedestrians; later accounts document 21 deaths and roughly 150 injuries. The disaster can seem impossible until the speed and force of a sudden industrial tank failure are understood. Beyond its bizarre headline, it tells a serious story about engineering safety and the consequences of poor oversight.
stories.sourceTitle: Smithsonian Magazine: Great Molasses Flood

stories.title: A strange repeating signal turned out to be a stellar remnant
stories.summary: Jocelyn Bell Burnell spotted an extremely regular radio pulse in 1967. It led to the discovery of pulsars, rapidly spinning neutron stars.
stories.full: Working with radio telescope records at Cambridge in 1967, graduate student Jocelyn Bell Burnell identified a signal repeating with extraordinary regularity. The researchers jokingly entertained the possibility of an artificial signal before finding others and understanding the astronomical explanation. Pulsars are rapidly rotating neutron stars that sweep radiation beams across space like lighthouses. NASA recounts how a small oddity in data revealed an entirely new class of observable objects.
stories.sourceTitle: NASA: Fifty years after pulsar discovery

stories.title: The U.S. Army sent fake tanks to war
stories.summary: During World War II, the 23rd Headquarters Special Troops used inflatable vehicles, recorded sounds and fake radio traffic to deceive enemy forces.
stories.full: A special American military unit known as the Ghost Army created convincing fake formations in Europe during World War II. Its members used inflatable tanks, false radio messages, sound equipment and theatrical impersonation to make enemy reconnaissance misjudge the location and strength of actual troops. Historians document dozens of deception maneuvers. The unit's name sounds supernatural, but its work involved practical psychology, stagecraft and battlefield intelligence.
stories.sourceTitle: National WWII Museum

stories.title: The boat Nikola Tesla steered without a wire in 1898
stories.summary: At a New York electrical exhibition in 1898, Nikola Tesla demonstrated a small boat responding to commands sent through the air. The startling part was not Tesla's reputation: it was a moving machine obeying a distant operator without a steering cable.
stories.full:
Picture a small boat changing direction while its operator stands away from it, without a physical steering line. In 1898, Tesla publicly demonstrated just such a vessel in New York. It was a practical example of wireless control, not merely an experiment with lighting or electric motors.

The Library of Congress preserves a research guide and newspaper trail documenting the demonstration. That trail lets readers investigate the actual event rather than read another generic account of Tesla's life. It is an early chapter in the long history of remote-controlled machines.
stories.sourceTitle: Library of Congress · Nikola Tesla research guide
stories.detail: A remote-controlled boat followed wireless commands at a public exhibition.

stories.title: A French pocket sundial reportedly surfaced in an Indiana field
stories.summary: A portable French sundial made in the 1600s was reportedly found while a doctor plowed a field in Indiana around 1860. Centuries and an ocean separated its manufacture from its supposed discovery, leaving a museum mystery for researchers to investigate.
stories.full:
A Smithsonian curator looking through the records for a seventeenth-century portable sundial noticed a strange piece of its history. The paperwork said that a doctor had reportedly uncovered it while plowing land in Indiana in 1860. Why would such an object be there?

The team followed the name in the records, identified a plausible local doctor, and involved a specialist in historic sundials. The account is fascinating precisely because the paper trail raises a question rather than proving every step of the instrument's journey. The find is reported, not an established account of how it crossed the Atlantic.
stories.sourceTitle: Smithsonian National Museum of American History · Pocket sundial inquiry
stories.detail: A 1600s French sundial had records claiming a nineteenth-century Indiana field discovery.

stories.title: The movie studio that rotated to chase the sunlight
stories.summary: Before electric movie lighting became routine, Edison's Black Maria studio was built with an opening roof and a rotating base. Crews could turn the building toward the sun, turning the entire studio into a tool for making motion pictures.
stories.full:
In the early 1890s, capturing motion pictures needed bright light. At West Orange, New Jersey, Edison's team constructed a studio with an unusual solution: its roof could open and the building could pivot to face the sun.

The dark structure became known as the Black Maria because it resembled a police wagon. The Library of Congress documents how this movable building helped early filmmakers record a steady stream of subjects. It was not an ordinary theater or an artificial-light stage; the architecture itself was part of the camera setup.
stories.sourceTitle: Library of Congress · Early Motion Picture Productions
stories.detail: The Black Maria motion picture studio was constructed to pivot toward sunlight.

stories.title: A filmed sneeze survived because it was registered as a photograph
stories.summary: Fred Ott sneezed for an Edison camera in 1894. Motion pictures did not yet have their own copyright registration category, but a photographic print of the brief scene was registered, helping preserve a tiny and unusual landmark of early cinema.
stories.full:
A sneeze lasting only moments became part of American film history. An Edison employee, Fred Ott, was filmed sneezing, and the resulting images traveled through a legal system that had not caught up with the new medium.

The Library of Congress describes a mounted photographic print received by the Copyright Office in January 1894. At that time, movie film did not have a normal registration category, so the surviving record was handled as a photograph. This is a story about an improvised solution to a brand-new kind of moving image, not simply a famous film title.
stories.sourceTitle: Library of Congress · Edison kinetoscopic record of a sneeze
stories.detail: A copyright office accepted the early motion picture record as a photograph.

stories.title: The wartime pigeon whose museum label left unanswered questions
stories.summary: The carrier pigeon Cher Ami became a celebrated World War I animal. Later researchers looking through museum records found that key details in the popular account, including how the bird's sex was recorded, were not backed by the surviving paperwork.
stories.full:
Cher Ami's preserved body became a museum artifact after the First World War. Over time, the bird's extraordinary wartime story appeared in exhibits and retellings, but historians continued examining what documents actually survived.

A Smithsonian investigation traced an influential 1920 memorandum and compared it with other Army and museum records. The surviving documentation does not settle every familiar claim. This is a story about how one label and an incomplete archive can shape the history people repeat. The Smithsonian makes the evidence and its uncertainties visible.
stories.sourceTitle: Smithsonian · Solving a 100-Year-Old Mystery About a Pigeon
stories.detail: Museum records and a 1920 memorandum left aspects of Cher Ami's popular story unresolved.

stories.title: The steel ball lowered into a largely unseen ocean
stories.summary: In June 1930, researchers off Bermuda began a daring descent inside the bathysphere, a compact steel sphere lowered by cable. It offered a direct view of deep-sea life that ships on the surface could not provide.
stories.full:
On a barge near Bermuda in June 1930, a suspended metal sphere swung out over the ocean. The bathysphere was less like a submarine than a tiny windowed chamber at the end of a long cable, built for people to descend and see deep water with their own eyes.

Historians of science recount the preparation, limitations and unexpected possibilities of these first descents. The unusual invention was a collaboration between engineering and natural-history curiosity: nobody had to pretend the researchers had already mapped the deep sea. Their goal was to observe what no surface traveler could see.
stories.sourceTitle: Smithsonian Magazine · Inside the First Deep-Sea Dive in History
stories.detail: The 1930 bathysphere used a cable-suspended steel chamber for direct undersea observation.

stories.title: The tiny switch that helped save Apollo 12 after lightning struck twice
stories.summary: Thirty-six seconds after Apollo 12 lifted off in 1969, lightning disrupted spacecraft readings. A second strike followed. Mission Control engineer John Aaron recognized a little-used electrical-system setting, and astronaut Alan Bean moved the SCE switch to AUX. The crew continued toward the Moon.
stories.full:
Apollo 12 had scarcely cleared the launch pad when the Saturn V encountered a problem mission planners did not want to see: lightning. Instrument readings became confusing, then another electrical discharge hit seconds later. The booster kept flying, but the team needed reliable spacecraft telemetry to tell what had happened.

In Mission Control, engineer John Aaron recognized that the Signal Conditioning Equipment could be restored by selecting its auxiliary setting. Alan Bean located and changed the switch aboard the spacecraft. NASA's records describe a recovery accomplished by one precise operational decision amid an enormous launch. Apollo 12 went on to land on the Moon, but its earliest moments remain a striking example of overlooked engineering knowledge.
stories.sourceTitle: NASA · 55 Years Ago: Apollo 12 Makes a Pinpoint Landing on the Moon
stories.detail: John Aaron identified the SCE-to-AUX correction after Apollo 12's lightning strikes.

stories.title: The shipwreck mechanism that calculated eclipses with ancient gears
stories.summary: A corroded mechanism recovered from an ancient shipwreck near the Greek island of Antikythera turned out to be a sophisticated geared instrument. The Smithsonian identifies it as the oldest known device designed to predict astronomical positions and eclipses.
stories.full:
The remarkable object did not look much like a modern calculator. It was a battered assembly of ancient mechanical parts found in the wreck of a ship near Antikythera. Researchers came to recognize its complex gearwork as an instrument for following astronomical cycles and predicting celestial events.

The surprising point is not an unsupported claim about lost modern technology. It is that ancient makers had built a specialized mechanical calculation device long before electronic machines existed. The Smithsonian's National Museum of American History preserves a modern reconstruction donated by historian Derek de Solla Price in 1979. The replica helps show how physical gears can encode mathematical relationships while the damaged original still invites investigation.
stories.sourceTitle: Smithsonian National Museum of American History · Antikythera mechanism replica
stories.detail: An ancient shipwreck preserved a gear-driven device used to predict astronomical positions and eclipses.

stories.title: A sound recording that waited about 150 years to be heard
stories.summary: In the nineteenth century, Édouard-Léon Scott de Martinville's phonautograph traced sound waves without a way to play them. Modern researchers converted surviving traces into audio in 2008, revealing sounds recorded long before conventional sound playback became possible.
stories.full:
Scott de Martinville's phonautograph was designed to draw the shape of a sound. A vibrating stylus marked soot-darkened surfaces, leaving a physical record of movement rather than something a nineteenth-century listener could play back. The original aim was investigation of acoustics, not a music player.

More than a century later, digital imaging and reconstruction made the apparently silent drawings audible. Researchers played back an 1860 recording of a French song in 2008, according to the Library of Congress. It is an unusual historical reversal: the sound had been stored first, and the means to hear it had to be invented much later. The object was not a lost recording machine with a hidden speaker; it was a visual trace finally interpreted as sound.
stories.sourceTitle: Library of Congress · From the Recording Registry: Phonautograms
stories.detail: Digital reconstruction in 2008 made an 1860 phonautograph trace audible.

stories.title: The telephone exhibition where an emperor helped test Bell's invention
stories.summary: Alexander Graham Bell's telephone was demonstrated to Emperor Pedro II of Brazil and scientist William Thomson at Philadelphia's 1876 Centennial Exhibition. A letter Bell wrote two days later describes his encounter and the demonstration in detail.
stories.full:
At the 1876 Centennial Exhibition, Alexander Graham Bell was showing an apparatus whose potential was not yet obvious to everyone. Emperor Pedro II of Brazil recognized Bell in the crowd and joined the group examining his work with scientist William Thomson, later Lord Kelvin.

Bell described the episode to his parents in a June 27 letter preserved by the Library of Congress. His account compares the costs and capabilities of electrical instruments on display, and it recounts moving into another room to sing into the telephone. The intriguing evidence is not a dramatic quotation repeated without context. It is a firsthand letter showing how a novel technology was demonstrated, compared with its rivals, and presented to influential witnesses before it became ordinary.
stories.sourceTitle: Library of Congress · Bell letter about the 1876 Centennial Exhibition
stories.detail: Bell documented the Centennial Exhibition telephone demonstration in a letter to his parents.

stories.title: The 1973 computer patent ruling that rewrote ENIAC's history
stories.summary: In 1973, a federal court invalidated the famous ENIAC computer patent. The judgment reopened questions about who had pioneered electronic computing, including crucial early work by John Atanasoff and Clifford Berry at Iowa State College.
stories.full:
The ENIAC was a landmark electronic computer developed at the University of Pennsylvania. Years afterward, a broad patent covering it sparked a dispute over who had built the underlying technologies first. Honeywell challenged claims held by Sperry Rand and introduced evidence of older electronic computing work.

In October 1973, U.S. District Judge Earl R. Larson invalidated the ENIAC patent. The ruling discussed ideas developed by John V. Atanasoff and Clifford Berry at Iowa State College before ENIAC. The court's decision does not reduce all of computing history to one inventor, but it demonstrates how patents, court documents and physical machines can complicate familiar origin stories.
stories.sourceTitle: University of Pennsylvania Archives · ENIAC Trial Exhibits
stories.detail: Judge Earl R. Larson invalidated the ENIAC patent in October 1973.

stories.title: The steamboat patent Abraham Lincoln filed before becoming president
stories.summary: In 1849, Abraham Lincoln received U.S. Patent No. 6,469 for a boat-lifting system using inflatable chambers. It was meant to help boats pass over shallow riverbeds without unloading cargo. The Smithsonian preserves Lincoln's wooden patent model; the device was never put into production.
stories.full:
Long before Abraham Lincoln occupied the White House, he knew the practical frustrations of river travel. Shallow riverbeds could stop cargo boats in their tracks. Lincoln proposed attaching expandable buoyant chambers to the sides of a vessel to raise it enough to pass through shoals. His patent was issued on May 22, 1849.

Lincoln made a scale model with assistance from a Springfield mechanic, and the original survives in the Smithsonian's collections. HISTORY's survey of famous inventors tells the story, while the Smithsonian model record and the original U.S. patent establish its technical details. Lincoln is the only U.S. president to have held a patent. There is no evidence his floating-device idea was manufactured for regular service.
stories.sourceTitle: Smithsonian National Museum of American History · Abraham Lincoln's Patent Model

sources.title: HISTORY · 7 Historical Figures You Didn't Know Were Inventors
US Patent No. 6,469 · Buoying Vessels over Shoals

stories.detail: Lincoln's inflatable-chamber boat invention received U.S. Patent No. 6,469 on May 22, 1849.
